This analysis is consistent with the well-known benefits of high efficiency cells coupled with low degradation rates [18]. Because of the assumed reduced degradation rate for the higher purity wafers from the Fz-CVD process, we can reduce the modeled efficiency to match that of the Siemens + Cz cells and still have a reduced LCOE at 120 µm/min poly-Si deposition rate. This shows that degradation rate is a strong lever for reducing LCOE for any technology. Figure 16. The other strong lever on cost is the poly-Si deposition rate. To understand the benefit of growth rates beyond the modeled 120 µm/min (possibly achieved, for example, using different precursors, or catalysts to increase reaction rates) we explored LCOE over a range of poly-Si deposition rates for the Fz-CVD process using the same analysis as above with DCAM and the comparative PV LCOE calculator. Figure 16 shows the relative LCOE between the base-case for the Siemens+Cz+TOPCon cell process and the Fz-CVD + Advanced TOPCon cell process. The Fz-CVD process has an improved LCOE for all growth rates above ~125 µm/min. Adding to this analysis we plotted the relative module price and relative installed system cost for Fz-CVD cells as a function of poly-Si deposition rate in Figure 17. Here the breakeven point (1 on each scale) is above 250 µm/min deposition rate for installed system costs and above 500 µm/min for module price (not shown in graph). However, as Figure 16 shows, even with more expensive module and system costs, the LCOE, with the assumptions given in Table III, for systems built from Fz-CVD wafers is competitive. The poly-Si deposition rate in the Fz-CVD reactor is a large lever for LCOE reduction, but tool and labor costs could also be significant due to the number of tools needed compared to the Siemens + Cz process.
